content: 1. Side effects or symptoms associated with the current contraceptive method, its administration, missed pills, or delayed injections should be carefully monitored and documented. This includes 54 specific recommendations for workflows, decision-making scenarios, and data requirements. 2. The Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) for Family Planning includes a structured approach to assess whether a client wishes to continue with their current contraceptive method, discontinue it, or switch to another method. It also determines if resupply or procedural interventions are necessary. 3. Reinforcing messages should be provided to clients, as outlined in decision-support tables found in Component 6 and Web Annex C.1.3. 4. The client’s initial preference for a contraceptive method should be recorded before conducting medical eligibility tests. This preference may be based on prior knowledge or selected after discussing all available options. 5. The location where the contraceptive method will be provided depends on the availability of stock and the skill level of the healthcare worker present. 6. Reviewing the client’s medical record is an essential step, although no data is recorded during this activity. 7. Healthcare providers must determine with reasonable certainty, based on the client’s responses to a pregnancy checklist, whether the client is not pregnant. 8. Pregnancy test results should be documented, and recommendations should be made based on the outcomes. 9. Informed consent must be obtained from the client before providing any family planning services. 10. If necessary, pelvic/genital examinations and STI/HIV laboratory tests should be conducted to ensure the client’s safety and suitability for the chosen contraceptive method. 11. The specific contraceptive method provided to the client, including supplies and instructions on its use, should be documented. 12. If the client is unable to receive their chosen contraceptive method, the reason for this should be clearly recorded. 13. A backup contraceptive method may be advised based on the client’s history, primary method choice, and the start date of the primary method. 14. Any questions or concerns raised by the client should be addressed, although no data is recorded during this activity. 15. Follow-up appointments should be recommended based on the client’s needs and the requirements of the chosen contraceptive method. 16. The recommended follow-up date should be documented to ensure continuity of care. 17. Emergency referrals should be made if urgent care is required, and any relevant clinical details should be included in referral notes to ensure continuity of care at the referral facility. 18. The DAK includes decision-support logic and algorithms that align with WHO guidelines, deconstructing family planning recommendations into clear inputs and outputs for digital decision-support systems. 19. Decision-support tables detail the business rules, data inputs, and outputs necessary to support family planning workflows. These tables are based on the Decision Model and Notation (DMN) standard. 20. Scheduling logic is integrated into the DAK to facilitate digital tracking of clients, ensuring that healthcare workers are aware of when follow-up visits are due based on the client’s chosen method or service provided. 21. The sensitivity of pregnancy tests available at the national and facility levels can impact follow-up scheduling and workflows. Guidance on test sensitivity should be followed to ensure accurate decision-making. 22. Any changes to decision-support logic should be carefully reviewed and agreed upon by in-country clinical experts, as incorrect logic can negatively impact the quality of care. 23. The DAK provides a comprehensive overview of decision-support tables and algorithms for family planning modules, ensuring alignment with WHO guidelines and expert-reviewed recommendations. 24. Local customization and configuration of the DAK may be necessary to align with national guidelines and contextual differences, including the inclusion of additional data elements or changes to response options. 25. Unique identifiers for clients and facilities, as well as administrative and geographic data, should be incorporated into digital systems to enhance tracking and decision-making. 26. The availability of diagnostic tests and contraceptive methods at healthcare facilities can influence workflows and the client’s experience with family planning services. 27. Counseling services, including those for reproductive health, nutrition, and HIV, may be integrated into family planning workflows, with group counseling sessions considered in some contexts. 28. The DAK emphasizes the importance of accurate and context-specific decision-support logic to improve the quality of care and ensure that healthcare workers are equipped with reliable tools for decision-making.
